messages.author: 84aac2580b195c68
messages.subject: Methods for checking the unidimensionality
parts:
Hello Phil,

While calibrating the items, are there any methods available for checking the unidimensionality of the data( i.e. response matrix ) other than factor analysis and using confirmatory mirt() function (where you get the loading matrix)?



Thanking you,

Irshad

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Methods for checking the unidimensionality
parts:
You don't have to use confirmatory models to check dimensionality, you can just use exploratory ones (pass a # to the model input). Comparing things like AIC and BIC are useful here, and will correspond quite well to a scree plot with a polychoric correlation matrix. See help(psych::fa.parallel.poly) for a limited information variant of this approach.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Methods for checking the unidimensionality

Thank you for the reply Phil.


Okay, now I understand that we do not need the confirmatory model to check the dimensionality .


Consider a scenario where there are two constructs/dimensions in the data. One construct is prominent in few items while other construct is prominent in remaining items. 

If I want to know which item is getting dominated by which item (while using factor analysis) I will use factor loading  matrix to see this. 

Now, are there any any other methods to see which item is dominated by which construct other than looking at factor loading matrix?




Thanking you,
Irshad

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Methods for checking the unidimensionality
parts: On Mon, Dec 22, 2014 at 10:59 PM, Irshad Mujawar <irshadmuj...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thank you for the reply Phil.

Suppose we have an item which is multidimensional. Now if we  are looking at the loading matrix, what threshold we should keep on the entries (correlation) in loading matrix to declare that particular item as multidimensional?

Depends on a lot of things, so there's no real cutoff value. Try a couple different cutoffs to see how the solution changes. This exact problem exists in the traditional exploratory factor analysis literature as well, so books on FA talk about this issue in depth as well (and why ridged cutoffs generally should be avoided).

Phil
